title: Cost Optimization
description: Reduce cloud spending without sacrificing performance or reliability. Learn right-sizing, instance purchasing options, storage tiers, idle resource cleanup, and cost monitoring techniques.

data.text: Cost optimization is not about cutting corners. It is about spending money wisely so that every dollar buys performance, reliability, or features. Senior engineers who understand cloud economics can build systems that are both powerful and affordable.

Cloud costs have a way of creeping up silently. Unattached storage, over-sized instances, and forgotten development environments are the most common culprits. Regular cost reviews catch these problems early.

Right-sizing means choosing the smallest resource that still meets your performance requirements. Start with the metrics: CPU utilization, memory usage, network throughput, and disk IOPS. If your server runs at 10% CPU on average, it is probably over-sized.

data.title: Right-Sizing Signals
items: CPU utilization consistently below 40% — consider downsizing
Memory utilization above 80% with swapping — upsize or optimize
Network throughput near the instance limit — choose a higher-bandwidth tier
Disk IOPS at the limit — move to a faster volume type

data.text: Cloud providers offer three main purchasing models. On-demand instances are flexible but expensive. Reserved instances commit you to one or three years for a discount. Spot instances use unused capacity at a steep discount but can be reclaimed with short notice.

Not all data needs to be stored on fast, expensive disks. Storage tiers let you match cost to access patterns. Hot storage is for frequently accessed data. Warm storage is for data accessed occasionally. Cold or archive storage is for data you rarely need but must keep.

data.title: Storage Tier Strategy
items: Hot: active database, cache, recent user uploads
Warm: backups from the last 30 days, logs for active debugging
Cold: backups older than 30 days, compliance archives
Archive: long-term retention for legal or audit requirements

data.text: Development environments, test databases, and unused load balancers accumulate quickly. Automated cleanup policies remove resources after a period of inactivity. Tagging everything with owner, project, and environment makes cleanup scripts safe and effective.

data.title: Hidden Cost
data.text: Data transfer between cloud regions or between cloud and on-premises can cost more than compute. Design your architecture to minimize cross-region data movement, and use peering or dedicated connections where transfer is unavoidable.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Right-size based on actual utilization metrics, not peak estimates
Use reserved instances for predictable workloads and spot instances for batch jobs
Match storage tiers to access patterns: hot, warm, cold, and archive
Automate cleanup of idle resources with tagging policies
Monitor data transfer costs — they often exceed compute costs
data.takeaway: Cost optimization is a continuous process, not a one-time task. Review spending monthly and involve the whole team.

items.question: How do I get visibility into cloud costs?
items.answer: Enable cost allocation tags and use your cloud provider's cost explorer. Set budget alerts at 80% and 100% of your monthly forecast. Tools like Kubecost or OpenCost help for Kubernetes environments.

items.question: Should I always use spot instances to save money?
items.answer: Only for fault-tolerant workloads. If a task can be safely interrupted and retried, spot instances are ideal. For stateful services or user-facing APIs, use reserved or on-demand instances.

items.question: What is the biggest source of wasted cloud spend?
items.answer: Unused or unattached resources: EBS volumes, Elastic IPs, load balancers with no backends, and idle RDS instances. Automated audits and lifecycle policies catch most of these.

data.title: Cost Audit for a Growing Startup
data.description: A startup's cloud bill has grown from $2,000 to $18,000 per month in six months. The team has not reviewed costs systematically. Conduct a cost audit: categorize the spend, identify the top three drivers, and propose a cost optimization plan with estimated savings.
data.expectedOutcome: A cost audit report with categorized spend, top cost drivers, a prioritized optimization plan, and estimated monthly savings for each recommendation.
